title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest spans your five tracked topics — anti-aging (with a look beyond supplements at topicals/procedures), HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, HER2+/TP53 (p53-gene) breast cancer, and sleep. Highlights include a fresh p53-reactivation drug milestone, Enhertu's move into early HER2+ disease, and a reframing of "disjointed" sleep around day-to-day regularity. Sources from PubMed/PMC, Nature, NEJM (via PMV), Frontiers, eLife, and the AASM are linked as chips below each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.body:
Two threads this morning: fresh human data on **urolithin A** for immune aging, and a look beyond pills at **exosome-based topicals/procedures**.

- **Urolithin A rejuvenates aging immune cells.** A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in *Nature Aging* (50 healthy adults 45–70, **1,000 mg/day for 28 days**; NCT05735886) found this mitophagy inducer expanded **naive, less-exhausted CD8+ T cells**, shifted immune-cell metabolism toward mitochondrial (fatty-acid) oxidation, and improved monocyte bacterial clearance — with side effects no different from placebo. It's a small, short, mechanism-focused study, so treat it as a promising signal, not proof of clinical benefit.
- **Coming soon (glucose metabolism).** The **NIA (NIH)** trial testing urolithin A on insulin secretion and mitochondrial function in adults 55+ (NCT06274749) is set to begin enrolling **Aug 25, 2026** — worth watching for harder metabolic endpoints.
- **Topicals & procedures — exosomes.** A 2026 systematic review (21 studies, *Dermatology Practical & Conceptual*) reports **exosome-based skin treatments** improve elasticity, reduce wrinkle depth, boost hydration, and increase collagen/elastin synthesis. A companion review of **microneedling + exosomes** found split-face gains over microneedling alone (e.g., wrinkle roughness down ~12–14% vs ~7%, elasticity +11% vs −3%). Caveats are real: **small trials, ≤6-month follow-up, and undisclosed regulatory status** of many exosome products.

Practical framing: prefer interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and be cautious with cosmetic "exosome" offerings whose sourcing and purity aren't documented.

sections.body:
This week's evidence keeps HIIT a **time-efficient** metabolic tool for women — while pushing back on the idea that it's always superior to steadier cardio.

- **PCOS: HIIT isn't clearly better than MICT.** A 2025 PRISMA meta-analysis of RCTs (*Frontiers in Endocrinology*) directly comparing **HIIT vs. moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)** in premenopausal women with PCOS found **no significant superiority** of either across body composition, VO2max, glucose/insulin, lipids, or hormones (low-to-very-low certainty). Bottom line: pick the modality you'll actually adhere to.
- **Low-volume HIIT can match longer MICT.** In older women with type 2 diabetes, a 12-week RCT found **~75 min/week of low-volume HIIT** produced similar drops in total and trunk fat and gains in lean mass as **150 min/week of MICT**, and improved post-exercise glucose on continuous monitoring — meaningful when time is the main barrier.
- **Bodyweight HIIT works, no gym needed.** A 2026 RCT of **low-cost, bodyweight HIIT** (40-min sessions, 3×/week, 8 weeks) in older adults with metabolic syndrome (36 of 40 participants women) improved **VO2max (~20%)** and cut blood pressure, fasting glucose (−32%), HbA1c (−35%), and triglycerides (−39%).

Bottom line: intensity drives cardio and metabolic wins, but **adherence and pairing with resistance training** matter more than HIIT-vs-MICT dogma. Progress volume gradually and keep recovery adequate.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the evidence-based, **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Two 2026 meta-analyses refine *how* to get the most from it.

- **Adding biofeedback + electrical stimulation helps.** A 2026 meta-analysis in the *International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics* (20 RCTs, **2,421** women with postpartum SUI) found **biofeedback electrical stimulation (BFES) + PFMT** outperformed either BFES or PFMT alone — improving clinical response, **pelvic-floor muscle strength**, muscle-fiber potential, and reducing daily leakage episodes. (Heterogeneity and some publication bias mean interpret cautiously.)
- **Technique, intensity, and supervision.** A 2026 systematic review & meta-analysis presented at the **International Continence Society** (19 RCTs) confirmed PFMT significantly improves incontinence and muscle strength postpartum, with **PFMT-only and PFMT-plus-adjuncts comparably effective** — reinforcing that **correct activation and consistency** matter as much as the add-ons.

Key point: confirm you're truly contracting the pelvic floor (a clinician or biofeedback can verify), train consistently, and consider adding **electrical stimulation/biofeedback** if progress stalls. Supervised programs generally beat unsupervised ones.

sources.title: Biofeedback electrical stimulation combined with pelvic floor muscle training on postpartum stress urinary incontinence: a meta-analysis

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 (p53) Breast Cancer
sections.body:
A landmark week for the **p53 gene**: for the first time, a drug directly *reactivates* a mutant p53 — plus a major HER2+ approval and an integrative angle on drug resistance.

- **First-in-class p53 reactivator (rezatapopt).** *NEJM* published the first-in-human Phase 1 of **rezatapopt (PC14586)**, an oral small molecule that binds the pocket created by the **TP53 Y220C** mutation and restores wild-type tumor-suppressor function — 77 heavily pretreated patients, manageable toxicity, and genuine responses (median duration ~8 months). Interim **Phase 2 PYNNACLE** data (NCT04585750) report an **18% response rate in the breast-cancer cohort**, with a dedicated **HER2+ subgroup**. This is the first time pharmacologic p53 reactivation has produced clinical responses.
- **Enhertu moves into early HER2+ disease.** The FDA approved **trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd / Enhertu)** for **neoadjuvant and adjuvant** treatment of early-stage HER2+ breast cancer (DESTINY-Breast11 and -Breast05) — extending this potent antibody-drug conjugate beyond the metastatic setting.
- **Integrative angle — senolytics after ADC resistance.** A 2026 *Scientific Reports* study found deruxtecan-based ADCs can drive **cancer-cell senescence via the p53/p21 axis** (a resistance mechanism), providing rationale to pair or follow ADCs with **senolytic/senomorphic agents** to clear these dormant cells.

Important framing: "alternative" here means **evidence-based options discussed with your oncology team** — not a replacement for HER2-targeted therapy. Rezatapopt and senolytic strategies remain investigational; germline TP53 mutations also warrant genetics/family-risk counseling.

sections.body:
For **restless or disjointed** sleep, a useful reframing this morning: *when* and *how consistently* you sleep may matter as much as how long.

- **Regularity beats duration.** UK Biobank analyses using the **Sleep Regularity Index (SRI)** — day-to-day consistency of sleep-wake timing from accelerometers — found the **most irregular** sleepers had ~1.5× higher all-cause mortality vs. average, and higher regularity tracked with **20–48% lower** all-cause mortality. Notably, **regularity predicted mortality more strongly than sleep duration**. For fragmented schedules, a **fixed wake time** is a high-leverage fix.
- **Behavioral therapy stays first-line.** The AASM's 2026 combination-treatment guideline reaffirms **CBT-I** as the anchor: CBT-I + medication beats medication alone, but is **not** better than **CBT-I alone**.
- **Medications & supplements, honestly.** Among drugs, **dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** like **daridorexant** are increasingly favored for chronic insomnia — sustained benefit on night-time symptoms and daytime function with a **lower dependence/misuse profile** than older hypnotics. On supplements: **melatonin** helps mainly **circadian** problems (jet lag, shift work), not chronic insomnia; evidence for **magnesium** remains limited.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time** every day (regularity first).
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If disruption persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
